etymology: From Old French tabour (a small drum), a diminutive of the same root that gives us tabor; rendering the Hebrew toph — a hand-drum or timbrel stretched with skin, struck and shaken in feast and procession.
biblical_def: The tabret is the small hand-drum of the Hebrews, the toph, carried in the hand and beaten to mark rejoicing (Gen 31:27). Laban chides Jacob that, had he not stolen away, he would have been sent off “with mirth, and with songs, with tabret, and with harp.” It sounds again in the prophetic company that Saul meets, coming down with “a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp” (1Sa 10:5), an instrument fit both for common feasting and for the raptures of prophecy. Yet Isaiah sets the tabret at the heart of a sober rebuke: “the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands” (Isa 5:12). Here the drum is not condemned, but the drunken deafness of men who make merry and never once lift their eyes to the God who made the day. When judgment falls, the first sound to die is this one: “The mirth of tabrets ceaseth” (Isa 24:8). The tabret thus measures a heart. Struck in thanksgiving to the LORD it is holy noise; struck to drown Him out it becomes the soundtrack of a feast that forgets its Maker.
webster_summary: A small hand-drum or timbrel used to mark rejoicing, feasting, and procession.
webster_full: TABRET, noun. A small drum or timbrel; a portable instrument of percussion consisting of a hoop stretched with skin, struck with the hand.
An instrument of mirth and festal rejoicing, named with harp, pipe, psaltery, and viol (Gen 31:27; 1Sa 10:5).
In Scripture, a sign of gladness whose ceasing marks the coming of judgment and desolation (Isa 24:8).
The Hebrew toph, cognate with the timbrel taken up by Miriam and the women at the sea (Exo 15:20).
Figuratively, the noise of a heart at ease, whether rightly rejoicing in the LORD or wrongly deaf to His works.
scriptures: Wherefore didst thou flee away secretly, and steal away from me; and didst not tell me, that I might have sent thee away with mirth, and with songs, with tabret, and with harp?

After that thou shalt come to the hill of God, where is the garrison of the Philistines: and it shall come to pass, when thou art come thither to the city, that thou shalt meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp, before them; and they shall prophesy:
Isa 5:12
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.
Isa 24:8
The mirth of tabrets ceaseth, the noise of them that rejoice endeth, the joy of the harp ceaseth.
corruption_summary: The tabret exposes a live corruption: the age’s pursuit of mirth and pleasure that never once regards the work of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah names the sin exactly: men whose feasts are full of harp and tabret and wine, “but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands” (Isa 5:12). This is not the abuse of a doctrine but the abuse of a gift — pleasure severed from the Giver, celebration with the eyes shut. Our own age has perfected the deaf feast: endless entertainment, a drumbeat that never stops, amusement engineered so that a soul need never think of God, of death, or of the operation of His hands. The tabret is innocent; the deafness is the crime.

The cure is not to break the drum but to open the ear. Miriam took a timbrel and led the women in praise of the LORD who triumphed gloriously (Exo 15:20); David appointed such instruments for the house of God. The same tabret that sounds a godless feast may sound a holy one. What Scripture rebukes is the mirth that regards not His work; what it commends is the rejoicing that begins and ends in Him — and it warns that when men will not still their revels to consider God, He will still them Himself, for “the mirth of tabrets ceaseth” (Isa 24:8).
roots_summary: Hebrew toph — a hand-drum or timbrel of festal rejoicing, rendered tabret and timbrel in the KJV.
roots_lines: Hebrew toph (H8596) — hand-drum, timbrel; rendered both “tabret” and “timbrel” in the KJV
From Old French tabour, diminutive tabret; the same family as the marching tabor
Named with harp, psaltery, pipe, and viol as an instrument of feasting and prophecy (1Sa 10:5)
First lifted in praise by Miriam and the women at the Red Sea (Exo 15:20)
Its silencing is a fixed prophetic sign of judgment on a merry-making people (Isa 24:8)
usage: They struck the tabret till dawn and never once regarded the work of the LORD — the very deafness Isaiah rebuked.
Miriam’s tabret and the drunkard’s tabret are the same wood and skin; the difference is the heart that beats them.
When a nation will not hush its tabrets to hear God, He hushes them Himself.

etymology: From Old French viole and Provençal viula, a stringed instrument played with a bow; in the KJV it renders the Hebrew nebel, a large stringed instrument or lute, elsewhere translated “psaltery.”
biblical_def: The viol renders the Hebrew nebel, a large stringed instrument of many notes, akin to the psaltery or lute. Isaiah lists it among the instruments of the careless feast: “the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts” (Isa 5:12). At the fall of the king of Babylon the same instrument follows him to the pit: “Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols” (Isa 14:11). Yet the sharpest word is Amos’s. To a people fat with religion and rotten with injustice, the LORD says, “Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amo 5:23). The very next chapter finds them “that chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David” (Amo 6:5) — men who ape David’s art while trampling David’s God. The viol is a good gift; David himself gave the pattern. But music offered by hands full of oppression is not worship — it is noise the LORD refuses to hear. The instrument that can lead a soul to heaven can also drug a conscience that means to keep its sins.
webster_summary: A stringed instrument played with a bow or plucked; the Hebrew nebel, a large lute or psaltery.
webster_full: VIOL, noun. A stringed musical instrument of six strings, played with a bow; anciently a large lute or psaltery.
In Scripture, the Hebrew nebel, a many-stringed instrument named among those used at feasts and in worship (Isa 5:12; Amo 6:5).
An instrument that may serve true praise after the pattern of David, or empty revelry divorced from righteousness.
Named at the funeral of Babylon’s pomp, its noise brought down to the grave (Isa 14:11).
Figuratively, music that the LORD refuses to hear when it rises from unjust hands (Amo 5:23).
scriptures: Isa 5:12
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.
Thy pomp is brought down to the grave, and the noise of thy viols: the worm is spread under thee, and the worms cover thee.
Amo 5:23
Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs; for I will not hear the melody of thy viols.
Amo 6:5
That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David;
corruption_summary: The viol names a live corruption: worship-music the LORD refuses to hear because it rises from lives emptied of justice and mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: “I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amo 5:23). God speaks these words to worshippers — men keeping feasts, singing songs, chanting to the viol like David. The corruption is not irreligion but religion hollowed out: skilled music, moving melody, and beneath it oppression of the poor and contempt for judgment. It is a live and present danger, for an age can master the craft of worship — the sound, the swell, the production — while the hands that lift the instrument are full of unrepented sin. God stops His ears at such music. He will not be flattered by melody from a heart that means to keep its idols.

The remedy is not less music but a changed life beneath it. Amos’s next command is the cure: “let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream” (Amo 5:24). The viol that God refuses at verse 23 He would gladly receive from a people whose worship and whose justice agree. David gave the true pattern — instruments invented for the praise of a God he feared and obeyed. To recover the viol is to recover that union: the melody offered by clean hands and a repentant heart, or else silenced, for God will not hear the song of the unjust.
roots_summary: Hebrew nebel — a large stringed instrument, rendered viol and psaltery in the KJV.
roots_lines: Hebrew nebel (H5035) — a large lute or harp of many strings; rendered “viol” and “psaltery”
From Old French viole, Provençal viula — a bowed or plucked stringed instrument
Named among the instruments of the careless feast (Isa 5:12) and of Babylon’s buried pomp (Isa 14:11)
Amos rebukes worship-music offered without justice: “I will not hear the melody of thy viols” (Amo 5:23)
David is invoked as the pattern of instruments rightly invented for praise (Amo 6:5)
usage: They chanted to the viol like David and robbed the poor like tyrants — and God would not hear the song.
A polished melody from an unrepentant heart is the very thing Amos says the LORD refuses.
The viol at Babylon’s grave preaches that pomp and music alike go down to the worm.

etymology: From Old French menestrel (a servant, entertainer, musician), from Late Latin ministerialis, one who ministers; in the KJV it renders the Hebrew participle menaggen (a player upon strings) and the Greek aulets (a flute-player).
biblical_def: A minstrel is one who plays upon an instrument, whether to soothe, to praise, or to mourn. The word appears twice in the KJV, and its two occurrences stand at opposite poles. In 2 Kings, Elisha, vexed by the presence of wicked Jehoram, calls for music before he will prophesy: “now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him” (2Ki 3:15). Here the minstrel is the servant of prophecy; the string is plucked and the Spirit descends, the soul quieted and lifted until the word of the LORD may flow. The second occurrence is a scene of grief and unbelief: when Jesus came into the ruler’s house, He “saw the minstrels and the people making a noise” (Mat 9:23), the hired mourners of a funeral He was about to overturn with resurrection. Between these two lies the whole use of the minstrel’s art. Rightly employed, music prepares a heart to receive God, as David’s harp refreshed Saul and drove the evil spirit away (1Sa 16:23). The Psalter commands it: “Praise the LORD with harp; sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings” (Psa 33:2). The minstrel’s calling is to make the string serve the glory of God and the good of the soul.
webster_summary: A player upon a musical instrument; a singer or musician who ministers by his art.
webster_full: MINSTREL, noun. A musician; one who plays upon an instrument or sings, formerly one who entertained in the households of the great.
In Scripture, a player upon strings whose music prepared Elisha to prophesy (2Ki 3:15).
Also the hired flute-players and mourners at a house of death (Mat 9:23).
From Late Latin ministerialis, one who ministers — the musician as a servant of others by his art.
Figuratively, any whose skill in music serves either the worship of God or the mere noise of men.
scriptures: But now bring me a minstrel. And it came to pass, when the minstrel played, that the hand of the LORD came upon him.
Mat 9:23
And when Jesus came into the ruler's house, and saw the minstrels and the people making a noise,
And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him.
Psa 33:2
Praise the LORD with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings.
corruption_summary: A musician’s office, not a contested doctrine; the word recovers music as a ministry that may serve God or degenerate into mere noise.
corruption_paragraphs: The two minstrels of Scripture set the standard and the warning side by side. Elisha’s minstrel plays and “the hand of the LORD” comes (2Ki 3:15); the ruler’s minstrels are “making a noise” over a girl the Lord of life is about to raise (Mat 9:23). The temptation the word rebukes is to reduce music to noise — performance for its own sake, sound that fills the ear and stirs the flesh but never quiets the soul before God. Much that passes for music in our day is exactly this: skillful, loud, and empty, a hired mourning that must be put out of doors before Christ can work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the minstrel’s true office — to minister. The very name comes from ministerialis, a servant. David’s harp served Saul’s troubled mind (1Sa 16:23); the temple singers served the praise of God (Psa 33:2); Elisha’s player served the coming of the word. Music is not an end but a handmaid, given to still the passions, lift the heart, and prepare a man to hear from heaven. Let the string be plucked to that end, and the minstrel is no idle entertainer but a servant of the living God.
roots_summary: Hebrew menaggen (a string-player) and Greek aulets (a flute-player) — the two words the KJV renders “minstrel.”

Greek aulets (G834) — a flute-player, of the hired mourners (Mat 9:23)

The Psalter commands such instruments in the worship of God (Psa 33:2)

Christ put the noisy minstrels out of the ruler’s house before He raised the dead; hired grief has no place where He works.
The minstrel is a minister by his very name — his string is meant to serve God and quiet men.

etymology: From Middle Dutch vierdekijn, a “little fourth,” a quarter of a barrel; in the KJV it renders the Greek metrts, a liquid measure of roughly eight or nine gallons.
biblical_def: A firkin is a measure of liquid, the Greek metrts, holding about eight or nine gallons. The word appears only once in Scripture, at the wedding in Cana: “there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece” (Joh 2:6). The Holy Ghost records the measure with deliberate care, for the sum is staggering. Six pots, each holding two or three firkins, yield something near one hundred and twenty gallons — and every drop, at Christ’s word, becomes wine: “Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim” (Joh 2:7). The firkin, then, is a vessel of divine abundance. Where the water of Jewish purifying stood, the wine of the new covenant now brims, poured out in a quantity no wedding could exhaust. Here is the God who deals in overflow: “my cup runneth over” (Psa 23:5), “able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Eph 3:20). The firkin measures not the stinginess of the world but the largeness of the Lord who turns the emptied pots of the old order into the running-over cup of grace, and does it, from the first, in firkins.
webster_summary: A liquid measure of roughly eight or nine gallons; a quarter of a barrel.
webster_full: FIRKIN, noun. A measure of capacity equal to the fourth part of a barrel; about eight or nine gallons.
In Scripture, the Greek metrts, the liquid measure of the six stone waterpots at Cana (Joh 2:6).
From Middle Dutch vierdekijn, a “little fourth” — a quarter portion.
A vessel of considerable capacity, marking the abundance of the water turned to wine.
Figuratively, a measure of the overflowing bounty of Christ, who fills to the brim.
scriptures: Joh 2:6
And there were set there six waterpots of stone, after the manner of the purifying of the Jews, containing two or three firkins apiece.
Joh 2:7
Jesus saith unto them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them up to the brim.
Psa 23:5
Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.
Eph 3:20
Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
corruption_summary: A liquid measure, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the largeness of Christ’s abundance against a grudging, stingy view of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the firkin rebukes is a small-hearted reckoning of God — the suspicion that grace is metered out grudgingly, that the Lord gives just enough and no more. Cana answers it in firkins. Six great pots filled to the brim, near a hundred and twenty gallons of the best wine, and all of it a wedding gift from the Son of God. Our age, calculating and mean in its estimate of God, forgets that He deals in overflow; it hoards and rations where He pours out. The firkin recalls the mind to a Lord whose cup runs over (Psa 23:5).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sheer abundance of Christ. The first of His signs was not a bare necessity but a lavish superabundance — more wine than the feast could drink, poured from vessels once reserved for ritual washing. He is “able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think” (Eph 3:20). The firkin, that humble Dutch quarter-barrel, becomes in John’s Gospel a measuring-cup for grace: not a trickle but a flood, filled up to the brim, from the God who is never stingy with His own.

Reckon God by the firkins of Cana, not by your own stingy arithmetic of grace.
The waterpots of purifying became pots of new wine, measured out in firkins of joy.

etymology: Hebrew maneh (a portion, a weight), from the root manah, to count or number; a standard weight, the mina, equal to fifty or sixty shekels, elsewhere in the KJV rendered “pound.”
biblical_def: The maneh is a fixed weight of silver, the mina, standing between the shekel and the talent. It appears by name once, in Ezekiel’s ordinance for the restored commonwealth: “the shekel shall be twenty gerahs: twenty shekels, five and twenty shekels, fifteen shekels, shall be your maneh” (Eze 45:12). The prophet fixes the standard because a nation is only as honest as its weights. Ezekiel’s vision of the new temple concerns itself not only with altars and courts but with the balances of the marketplace, for the God who is worshipped inside the sanctuary is the God who is robbed or honored at the scale outside it. The whole law is jealous for the just weight: “Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:36). Proverbs sets the matter as a plain moral test: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1). And the promise of long life in the land is bound to it: “a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened” (Deu 25:15). The maneh, a mere lump of metal on a balance, becomes a measure of the fear of God in a man’s dealings.
webster_summary: A Hebrew standard weight, the mina, of fifty or sixty shekels; rendered elsewhere “pound.”
webster_full: MANEH, noun. A Hebrew weight, the mina, equal to fifty or sixty shekels of silver; a standard of the balance.
In Scripture, the weight fixed by ordinance in Ezekiel’s temple vision (Eze 45:12).
From the Hebrew root manah, to count, number, or apportion.
A standard between the shekel and the talent, elsewhere translated “pound.”
Figuratively, the measure of honesty in trade, which the LORD requires and blesses.
scriptures: And the shekel shall be twenty gerahs: twenty shekels, five and twenty shekels, fifteen shekels, shall be your maneh.
Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
Pro 11:1
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
corruption_summary: The maneh names a live corruption: the false weight and rigged balance by which men rob their neighbors under a show of fairness.
corruption_paragraphs: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD” (Pro 11:1). The corruption is as old as commerce and as fresh as this morning’s transaction: the weight that reads heavier than it is, the measure short of what it claims, the fine print engineered to deceive. Ezekiel fixes the maneh precisely because dishonest men love an unfixed standard — a scale they can tilt, a definition they can shade to their profit. Our own age has multiplied the arts of the false balance: hidden fees, doctored figures, contracts written to rob, prices and promises that will not weigh out true. God calls it not a clever practice but an abomination.

Scripture names the sin plainly and requires its opposite: “a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have” (Deu 25:15). The just balance is not merely good business; it is a matter of the fear of God, for the same LORD who redeemed Israel from Egypt sets the standard of the scale: “I am the LORD your God” (Lev 19:36). To keep a true maneh is to confess that God sees the weight no customer checks. To keep a false one is to declare, in the coin of daily trade, that He does not. The recovery is a righteousness that weighs honestly when no man is watching, and reckons a just weight the delight of God.

etymology: From Old English fathm, the span of the outstretched arms, hence a measure of about six feet; in the KJV it renders the Greek orguia, the length from fingertip to fingertip of the extended arms, used to sound the depth of the sea.
biblical_def: A fathom is the measure of the outstretched arms, about six feet, the seaman’s reckoning of depth. It appears once in Scripture, in the terror of Paul’s shipwreck off Malta: “And sounded, and found it twenty fathoms: and when they had gone a little further, they sounded again, and found it fifteen fathoms” (Act 27:28). The sailors, driven fourteen nights in Adria and fearing the ship would strike, let down the lead to measure the water beneath the keel — twenty fathoms, then fifteen, the depth shoaling as the shore drew near. It is a small, exact detail in a great deliverance, for God had promised Paul the lives of all aboard, and the sounding-line traced the very edge of that promise. The fathom measures what men can measure of the deep — and thereby marks the boundary of what they cannot. The seaman reads twenty, then fifteen; but there are depths no lead can sound. “These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep” (Psa 107:24). And deeper than any sea is the counsel of God Himself: “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out” (Rom 11:33). The fathom is honest about its limits; it reaches the sea-bottom but never the bottom of God.
webster_summary: A measure of length equal to the span of the outstretched arms, about six feet, used to sound depths.
webster_full: FATHOM, noun. A measure of length containing six feet, the space to which a man may extend his arms; used chiefly in measuring the depth of water.
In Scripture, the Greek orguia, the sounding of the sea in Paul’s shipwreck (Act 27:28).
From Old English fathm, the embrace or span of the extended arms.
A depth taken by the lead and line, marking how near a vessel stands to bottom or shore.
Figuratively, the limit of what man can measure, against the unsearchable depths of God.
scriptures: And sounded, and found it twenty fathoms: and when they had gone a little further, they sounded again, and found it fifteen fathoms.
These see the works of the LORD, and his wonders in the deep.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
Psa 36:6
Thy righteousness is like the great mountains; thy judgments are a great deep: O LORD, thou preservest man and beast.
corruption_summary: A nautical measure of depth, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the humility that measures what it can and bows before what it cannot.
corruption_paragraphs: The temptation the fathom rebukes is the conceit that all things can be sounded — that given enough line, man can reach the bottom of every deep, God included. The modern mind trusts its instruments to measure everything and confesses no mystery it cannot in principle plumb. But the sailors in Adria, for all their skill with the lead, could measure only the water; the storm, the promise given to Paul, and the God who kept every soul aboard lay wholly beyond their sounding. The fathom is a rebuke to the pride that thinks the depths of God are just a longer measurement away.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is a reverent knowledge of our limits. The lead-line is good and honest work; twenty fathoms, then fifteen, is exactly the kind of measuring God gives men to do, and by it the mariners preserved the ship. But past the sea-floor lies a deep no line can reach: “thy judgments are a great deep” (Psa 36:6), and His ways are “past finding out” (Rom 11:33). To fathom the sea and adore the unfathomable God is wisdom; to imagine that what cannot be measured cannot be real is the fool’s short line.

The fathom measures the deep of the sea and confesses the deeper deep it cannot reach.
Fathom what you can; adore what you cannot — His judgments are past finding out.

etymology: Hebrew bath, a liquid measure equal to the ephah in dry goods, roughly six or seven gallons; the largest common Hebrew liquid measure, the tenth part of a homer.
biblical_def: The bath is the great Hebrew liquid measure, the counterpart of the dry ephah, holding some six or seven gallons and forming the tenth part of a homer (Eze 45:14). By it the molten sea of Solomon’s temple was reckoned: “it contained two thousand baths” (1Ki 7:26), a vast basin for the priests’ washing, its capacity told in this measure. Ezekiel binds the bath into the ordinances of oil for the restored worship: “the bath of oil, ye shall offer the tenth part of a bath out of the cor” (Eze 45:14), fixing the exact portion due to God. And in the parable of the unjust steward, the debtor’s hundred measures of oil (Luk 16:6) are baths, the very unit of that reckoning. Isaiah turns the measure into a threat of barrenness: “ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath” (Isa 5:10), a whole day’s ploughing of vines shrunk to a single measure — the curse on a fruitless people who have filled the land with iniquity. The bath thus serves both temple and marketplace, both worship and warning. It gauges the water of the priests’ cleansing, the oil of the offering, and, when God withdraws His hand, the pitiful yield of a vineyard He has ceased to bless.
webster_summary: The largest common Hebrew liquid measure, about six or seven gallons; the tenth of a homer.
webster_full: BATH, noun. A Hebrew measure of liquids, containing about six or seven gallons; the counterpart of the ephah in dry measure.

The unit of the hundred measures of oil in the parable of the steward (Luk 16:6).
Figuratively, the meager yield of a cursed vineyard, ten acres to one bath (Isa 5:10).
scriptures: And it was an hand breadth thick, and the brim thereof was wrought like the brim of a cup, with flowers of lilies: it contained two thousand baths.
Isa 5:10
Yea, ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath, and the seed of an homer shall yield an ephah.
Concerning the ordinance of oil, the bath of oil, ye shall offer the tenth part of a bath out of the cor, which is an homer of ten baths; for ten baths are an homer:
Luk 16:6
And he said, An hundred measures of oil. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty.
corruption_summary: A liquid measure of temple and market, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the exactness of what is due to God against a careless, unmeasured worship.
corruption_paragraphs: The bath rebukes the careless spirit that will not trouble to measure what it owes to God. Ezekiel fixes the ordinance to the exact tenth of a bath (Eze 45:14) because worship is not a matter of rough guesses and convenient rounding; the LORD names the portion, and it is to be rendered precisely. Our age loves an unmeasured religion — give what you feel, when you feel it, in whatever amount seems fitting — but Scripture ties the offering to a standard. Isaiah’s warning stands over the negligent: a vineyard that will not honor God yields, in the end, but one bath from ten acres (Isa 5:10), for He can shrink the harvest of a people who despise His measure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the exactness of holy things. The molten sea held two thousand baths of water for the priests’ cleansing (1Ki 7:26); the offering of oil was reckoned to the tenth of a bath (Eze 45:14); even the steward’s debts were told in this measure (Luk 16:6). God is not vague about what pertains to His house. To recover the bath is to recover the reverence that gives Him full measure — not the leftover, the rounded-down, the approximate, but the exact and honest portion, brimming as the great sea of the temple, from a heart that fears to shortchange its Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew bath — the largest common liquid measure, the tenth of a homer.
roots_lines: Hebrew bath (H1324) — a liquid measure of about six or seven gallons
The liquid counterpart of the dry ephah; the tenth part of a homer or cor (Eze 45:14)
Measured the molten sea of Solomon’s temple at two thousand baths (1Ki 7:26)
The Greek batos underlies the “measures” of oil in Luk 16:6
A figure of judgment when ten acres yield but one bath (Isa 5:10)
usage: The molten sea held two thousand baths — the temple deals in exact measure, not rough guesses.
Ezekiel fixes the oil to the tenth of a bath, for worship is rendered by God’s standard, not our whim.
Ten acres to one bath: God can shrink the vineyard of a people who despise His measure.

etymology: From Old English windan (to turn or twist) and stger (a flight of steps); rendering the Hebrew lulim, a spiral or turning stairway, a word occurring only here in Scripture.
biblical_def: The winding stairs are the spiral ascent within the wall of Solomon’s temple, by which the priests rose from floor to floor of the side chambers. The phrase renders the Hebrew lulim, found only once: “The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third” (1Ki 6:8). Around the sanctuary ran three tiers of chambers, and the way up was not a straight flight but a stair that turned as it climbed, hidden in the thickness of the wall, leading from the lowest story to the highest. It is a small architectural detail, yet the Spirit preserved it, and it preaches. The house of God is entered not at a leap but by an ascent, and the ascent turns — step upon step, from strength to strength: “they go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God” (Psa 84:7). The winding stair answers the great question of the sanctuary: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Psa 24:3). None climb to God carelessly or all at once; the way up is by degrees, turning ever toward the height, as Jacob saw the ladder set on earth whose top reached to heaven (Gen 28:12). The middle chamber is gained by the turning stair.
webster_summary: A spiral or turning stairway; the ascent within the wall of Solomon’s temple to its side chambers.
webster_full: WINDING STAIRS, noun. A stairway that turns or spirals as it ascends, as distinguished from a straight flight.
In Scripture, the turning stair within the temple wall, leading up to the middle and third chambers (1Ki 6:8).
From Old English windan, to turn or twist, and stger, a flight of steps.
Rendering the Hebrew lulim, a word occurring only once in the Scriptures.
Figuratively, the gradual, turning ascent of the soul toward the presence of God.
scriptures: The door for the middle chamber was in the right side of the house: and they went up with winding stairs into the middle chamber, and out of the middle into the third.
Psa 84:7
They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God.
Psa 24:3
Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place?
And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.
corruption_summary: An architectural detail of the temple, not a contested doctrine; it recovers the truth that the soul ascends to God by degrees, not by a leap.
corruption_paragraphs: The winding stair rebukes an age that despises slow ascent and demands the summit at once. We want instant maturity, immediate assurance, the top chamber without the turning steps — sanctification as an event to be seized rather than a stair to be climbed. But the temple was built otherwise. The way to the middle chamber turned and rose, story upon story, and the priest reached the height only by the patient tread of the spiral. To scorn the stair is to be forever on the ground floor, wishing oneself above.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is growth by degrees. The saints in Zion go “from strength to strength” (Psa 84:7), not from weakness to glory in a single bound; the hill of the LORD is ascended by those who set the foot to the turning step (Psa 24:3). Jacob’s ladder had its rungs between earth and heaven (Gen 28:12), and the temple’s stair had its turns between the floors. So it is with the Christian life: the middle chamber is gained by ascent, the ascent turns, and the LORD who set the stair within the wall of His house means His people to climb it, patiently, all the way up.
roots_summary: Hebrew lulim — a spiral stairway, occurring only at 1Ki 6:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew lulim (H3883) — a winding or spiral stair; KJV hapax at 1Ki 6:8
From Old English windan (to turn) and stger (a flight of steps)

Figures the gradual ascent to God: “from strength to strength” (Psa 84:7)
Echoes the great question of the sanctuary: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD?” (Psa 24:3)
usage: The middle chamber was gained by winding stairs — no one leaps to the height of the house of God.
Sanctification is a turning stair, story upon story, not a single bound to glory.
They go from strength to strength; the way up to God turns, and the saints tread every step.

etymology: From Latin pinnaculum, a little wing or peak, diminutive of pinna (a wing, point, or battlement); in the KJV it renders the Greek pterugion, a wing-like edge or summit, here the highest point of the temple.
biblical_def: A pinnacle is a wing-like summit or topmost point, the Greek pterugion, the highest edge of a building. In Scripture it names one exact place: the peak of the temple where Satan set the Lord Jesus in the second temptation. “Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple” (Mat 4:5); and Luke adds the tempter’s dare in full: “set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence” (Luk 4:9). The devil quoted Scripture as he tempted — the promise that angels would bear Him up — urging Christ to fling Himself from the height and force a miracle of rescue. Our Lord answered with the deeper word: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah” (Deu 6:16). The pinnacle is therefore the very stage of presumption. To stand upon it and leap is not faith but the counterfeit of faith — demanding that God prove His care on our own reckless terms, twisting a true promise (Psa 91:11) into a pretext for tempting Him. Christ would not cast Himself down; He would be cast down in God’s time, at Calvary, in obedience and not in show. The pinnacle marks the height at which faith becomes presumption if it will not wait on God.
webster_summary: A wing-like summit or highest point of a building; the peak of the temple in Christ’s temptation.
webster_full: PINNACLE, noun. A turret, or part of a building elevated above the main structure; a high, spiring point; a summit.
In Scripture, the highest point of the temple, whither Satan carried Christ (Mat 4:5).
From Latin pinnaculum, a little wing or peak, from pinna, a wing or battlement.
Rendering the Greek pterugion, a wing-like edge or extremity.
Figuratively, the height at which trust in God may be perverted into the sin of tempting Him.
scriptures: Mat 4:5
Then the devil taketh him up into the holy city, and setteth him on a pinnacle of the temple,
Luk 4:9
And he brought him to Jerusalem, and set him on a pinnacle of the temple, and said unto him, If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down from hence:
Deu 6:16
Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God, as ye tempted him in Massah.
For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.
corruption_summary: The pinnacle names a live corruption: presumption dressed as faith, the tempting of God by demanding He prove His care on our own terms.
corruption_paragraphs: On the pinnacle the devil dressed presumption as faith. He quoted a true promise — that angels would bear up the godly (Psa 91:11) — and urged Christ to prove it by a needless leap. This is a live and subtle corruption, for it wears the very language of trust. It says: if God loves me, let Him rescue me from the danger into which I have deliberately thrown myself; let Him work the miracle I demand, on the schedule I set, or His care is in doubt. Whole movements now teach believers to “name and claim,” to test God by casting themselves from spiritual heights and insisting He catch them. It is not faith. It is the sin of Massah.

Christ named it plainly: “Ye shall not tempt the LORD your God” (Deu 6:16). The corruption is answered not by doubting God’s promises but by refusing to abuse them. True faith trusts God in the way He appoints and does not manufacture crises to compel His hand. The angels do keep the godly in all their ways (Psa 91:11) — their ways, the paths of obedience, not the reckless leaps of self-will. Christ would not cast Himself from the pinnacle to make a show; He would go down to death in God’s time and God’s way. To recover the pinnacle is to see that demanding proof of God’s care on our own terms is not the height of faith but the counterfeit of it.
roots_summary: Greek pterugion, Latin pinnaculum — a wing-like summit, the peak of the temple.

etymology: From Middle English celen (to line or panel a room), likely from Latin caelum or Old French celer; the KJV spells it “cieled,” meaning to overlay walls or roof with wood, especially costly panelled work.
biblical_def: To be ceiled — spelled “cieled” in the KJV — is to be lined or panelled with wood, the finished woodwork of a costly house. It carries a double weight in Scripture, honor and rebuke. Rightly used, it adorns the house of God: Solomon “cieled” the greater house of the temple with fir, overlaid with fine gold and set with palm trees and chains (2Ch 3:5) — lavish beauty spent upon the dwelling of the LORD. But wrongly loved, the same panelling becomes a monument to self. Jeremiah condemns the king who builds by unrighteousness: “I will build me a wide house and large chambers … and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion” (Jer 22:14) — luxury raised on injustice, cedar and paint while the poor are oppressed. Sharpest of all is Haggai’s word to the returned exiles who had panelled their own homes and left the temple in ruins: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). There it is, the exposed heart of a people who lavish upon themselves what they will not spend upon God. He blows upon their gain and asks why: “Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house” (Hag 1:9). The ceiled house measures where a man’s treasure truly lies.
webster_summary: Lined or overlaid with wood; the panelled finish of a costly house or of the temple.
webster_full: CEILED, participle. Overlaid or lined with wood; furnished with a ceiling or wainscot of panelled work. KJV spelling: “cieled.”
In Scripture, the fir-panelling of the temple, overlaid with gold (2Ch 3:5).
Also the cedar-panelled luxury of a house built by unrighteousness (Jer 22:14).
The self-indulgent comfort rebuked by Haggai while God’s house lay waste (Hag 1:4).
Figuratively, the finished ease of self-comfort weighed against the honor due to God.
scriptures: That saith, I will build me a wide house and large chambers, and cutteth him out windows; and it is cieled with cedar, and painted with vermilion.
And the greater house he cieled with fir tree, which he overlaid with fine gold, and set thereon palm trees and chains.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Hag 1:9

Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little; and when ye brought it home, I did blow upon it. Why? saith the LORD of hosts. Because of mine house that is waste, and ye run every man unto his own house.
corruption_summary: The ceiled house names a live corruption: self-comfort set above the honor of God, panelling our own walls while His house lies waste.
corruption_paragraphs: Haggai names the sin without a caveat: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). The corruption is the quiet, respectable idolatry of self-comfort — men who spare no expense on their own ease and have nothing left, in money or zeal, for the house of God. It is a live and present sin, perhaps the reigning sin of a prosperous church age: finished basements and empty sanctuaries, lavish private comfort and a neglected work of God, every man running unto his own house (Hag 1:9). The cedar is not the crime; the crime is loving it above the LORD.

God’s answer is to blow upon the hoarded gain: “Ye looked for much, and, lo, it came to little … I did blow upon it” (Hag 1:9). The comfort men set above His honor He empties of blessing, that they might learn where their treasure belongs. The recovery is not to despise the panelled house — Solomon rightly ceiled the temple with fir and gold (2Ch 3:5) — but to put first things first. Panelling raised on injustice, as with Jeremiah’s king (Jer 22:14), or preferred above the ruined house of God, as with Haggai’s exiles, is under the divine rebuke. Let a man ceil his house if he will; but let him build the LORD’s house first, and love the honor of God above the finish of his own walls.
roots_summary: Middle English celen — to line or panel a room with wood; KJV spelling “cieled.”
roots_lines: Middle English celen, to line or panel; KJV consistently spells it “cieled”
Possibly from Latin caelum or Old French celer — to overlay or cover
Used of the temple’s honor: fir-panelling overlaid with fine gold (2Ch 3:5)
Used of sinful luxury: cedar and vermilion built by unrighteousness (Jer 22:14)

Solomon ceiled the temple with fir and gold; the exiles ceiled themselves and forgot the LORD.
God blew upon their hoarded comfort, for they had set their own walls above His honor.
